title: Sterlite Technologies and HFCL Ride the AI Data Centre Wave With Billions in Orders
excerpt: Two Indian optical fibre companies have emerged as unlikely AI winners, securing massive contracts to wire data centres in India and the US as hyperscaler spending accelerates.
body:
• Sterlite Technologies subsidiary secured a $1.11 billion (₹10,000 crore) multi-year contract from a US hyperscaler to supply optical connectivity products for AI data centre build-outs from FY27 to FY29
  • HFCL reported its strongest-ever April-June quarter with revenue more than doubling on AI-driven demand, as founder Mahendra Nahata likened the data centre construction wave to a "tsunami"
  • An equal-weighted index of 28 Indian data centre supply chain companies has added $48 billion in market value in 2026—a 45% gain while the broader Nifty 500 lost $300 billion
  • US hyperscale cloud providers have committed roughly $57 billion in India data centre capacity over the past year, while Adani and Reliance have pledged $100 billion to digital infrastructure

The Billion-Dollar Cable Play

Every AI query runs through a data centre. Every data centre runs on cables. Two Indian companies are now positioned at the centre of that wiring boom.

https://x.com/KaustubhYeole/status/2091064220615950351

Sterlite Technologies, the Vedanta Group-owned optical fibre maker, saw its stock surge 500% this year after its subsidiary secured a Product Award Letter worth approximately $1.11 billion (₹10,000 crore) from a US hyperscale cloud provider. The multi-year contract covers the supply of optical connectivity products for AI data centre build-outs from FY27 through FY29, according to company filings reported by ScanX Trade.

HFCL, the telecom equipment maker that wired much of India's 5G rollout, has pivoted to the same opportunity. The company reported its strongest-ever April-to-June quarter, with revenue more than doubling on AI-driven demand.

"In the past, we might have added capacity every three or five years. Now, it's a routine task."

— Mahendra Nahata, Founder, HFCL, likening the data centre construction wave to a "tsunami"

India's Hidden AI Winners

Sterlite and HFCL are the most visible examples of a broader phenomenon. An equal-weighted Bloomberg index of 28 Indian companies that feed the data centre ecosystem—makers of transformers, switchgear, wires, cables, and cooling systems—has added approximately $48 billion in combined market value in 2026, a rise of nearly 45%, according to The Hindu Business Line. The benchmark Nifty 500, by contrast, has lost over $300 billion in the same period.

TD Power Systems' shares have risen 68% on expectations of growing demand from AI facilities. MTAR Technologies has benefited from orders for power units used in fuel cell systems serving major tech operators. Sterlite itself has surged 500% this year, while HFCL has jumped 176%.

The Hyperscaler Spending Wave

The capital commitments underwriting this boom are enormous. Amazon plans to invest $12.7 billion in Indian cloud infrastructure through 2030. Google is deploying approximately $15 billion on an AI infrastructure hub in Visakhapatnam. A Reliance Industries joint venture signed an $11 billion data centre construction deal, while AdaniConnex has partnerships with Google and Uber for facility construction.

Over the past year, US hyperscale cloud providers have committed roughly $57 billion in Indian data centre capacity, according to an AFP review of financing announcements. Indian conglomerates Adani Group and Reliance Group have pledged $100 billion to digital and infrastructure projects. L&T recently secured a mega order—estimated between ₹10,000 and ₹15,000 crore—to build India's largest single-cluster AI factory in Chennai for US-based Together AI.

Risks and Reality Checks

Analysts warn that valuations across the sector have become stretched. Data Center Watch, the tracking arm of AI intelligence firm 10a Labs, found that at least 75 US projects worth around $130 billion were delayed or blocked in Q1 2026. Opposition to energy-intensive data centre projects poses an additional risk, though India has so far encountered limited resistance compared to the US and Europe.

India holds nearly one-fifth of the world's data but accounts for less than 5% of global data centre capacity, a gap that provides structural runway for growth regardless of near-term sentiment. Indian executives acknowledge overseas risks but argue domestic demand will ultimately offset any slowdown.

The Investment Case

For investors, the thesis is simple: every dollar of AI spending requires a multiple of that in physical infrastructure—cables, cooling, power, land. India's manufacturing base in these components, built over decades for the telecom sector, is now being repurposed for a market growing at several multiples of its predecessor. Whether the current valuations fully price in that opportunity is the open question.
